title: The Trade Deal Is in Its 'Last Inches.' For H-1B Workers, That Could Be the Point
excerpt: US Ambassador Sergio Gor says the H-1B overhaul isn't targeting India, as Washington and New Delhi race to close a bilateral trade agreement that explicitly includes tech talent mobility.
body:
When US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor told Outlook Business this week that the ongoing review of the H-1B visa programme is "part of a broader overhaul" of America's immigration system — not a measure "specifically directed at India" — the reassurance landed on an audience that has heard plenty of reassurances before. For many NRIs and their families, the H-1B visa is a critical pathway, and any changes, even those framed as general overhauls, are closely watched for their potential impact on careers and family reunification.

What made this one different is what came with it. Gor confirmed that the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) is now down to finalising "the language that ultimately both sides will sign." In New Delhi last week, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal wrapped up three days of intensive negotiations that, by both sides' accounts, were "very productive."

## A deal measured in 'last inches'

The BTA has been in the works since February 2024, when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then-US President Donald Trump agreed on a framework during the first high-level contact of Trump's second term. India wants a tariff of around 18 per cent on its goods — lower than the rates facing Bangladesh, Vietnam, and other Asian competitors. In exchange, New Delhi would lower trade barriers and absorb more American goods.

The US Supreme Court's invalidation of Trump's sweeping reciprocal tariffs complicated the legal framework this spring, but negotiators are now working around it. "We're on the last inches of getting it done, and it's very positive," Secretary of State Marco Rubio told IANS on Saturday. India's trade minister Piyush Goyal echoed the sentiment from London: "The day that happens, the deal is on."

US Deputy Assistant Secretary Bethany Poulos Morrison put the ambition in numbers. Washington is "driving towards the goal of Mission 500 — $500 billion in trade by 2030, with a real sense of urgency," she said, noting that 2023 was already a "historic year" for bilateral trade. This ambitious target underscores the strategic importance both nations place on deepening economic ties, which inevitably involves the movement of skilled professionals.

## Where immigration enters the fine print

The trade deal explicitly covers strategic sectors — information technology, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, semiconductor supply chains — that employ the largest share of Indian H-1B holders. When the US Embassy in India posted on X that the partnership includes "energy security to tech talent exchanges," it was acknowledging what every immigration attorney in the Bay Area already knows: the people are part of the equation. For the Indian diaspora, particularly those in tech, this signals a recognition of their integral role in the economic relationship.

India has been pushing for several immigration-adjacent concessions alongside the BTA. Chief among them is a totalization agreement — a social security pact that would let short-term workers avoid contributing to the host country's retirement system. The US has 30 such agreements with other countries. India, despite sending more skilled workers to America than any other nation, is not among them. Indian IT companies estimate the pact would save them roughly $4 billion a year in US Social Security contributions. For the 7,300 tech workers who returned to India in the first half of 2024, it could mean the difference between recovering some retirement savings and losing them entirely, a significant concern for NRIs planning their financial futures.

But for the Indian professional navigating the current maze — a consulate backlog measured in months, a lottery now ranked by salary, a self-petition approval rate at a record low — the trade deal carries a different kind of weight. It signals that Washington views the Indian talent pipeline as a commercial asset worth protecting, not a regulatory gap worth closing. Gor's reassurance that H-1B changes are not "directed at any particular country" is diplomatic shorthand. The trade deal is where that claim gets tested, offering a glimmer of hope that the economic partnership will eventually translate into more stable and predictable immigration pathways for skilled Indian workers.
